purpose: Define the complete, compilable, verbatim shape and observable serde contract of monokl's search-command request/response cluster -- SearchOptions, SearchLimits, Language, SearchResponse, SymbolsResult, and DependentsResult -- per docs/spec/01-core-architecture.md Section 4 (lines 506-597, the SearchOptions/SearchLimits/Language/SearchResponse/SymbolsResult/DependentsResult declarations), so a developer implementing the search/symbols/dependents commands never has to guess a field, a derive, a default value, or which code path a given default actually takes effect on. This cluster's central, easy-to-miss risk is that SearchOptions and SearchLimits both carry a hand-written impl Default with specific, documented fallback values, while neither struct carries #[serde(default)] anywhere -- container-level or field-level -- meaning those Default impls are completely inert for JSON deserialize: a JSON object omitting a required field fails outright rather than falling back to the Default impl's value, and for the two fields where Option<T>'s own inherent leniency independently applies (SearchLimits.max_results, SearchLimits.max_tokens), an omitted key yields None on deserialize while SearchLimits::default() yields Some(50)/Some(20_000) -- two different fallback values for the same 'caller didn't specify' intent, depending entirely on which code path constructs the value. This spec also locks Language, whose rename_all = "lowercase" rule produces a real, non-hypothetical divergence from "camelCase" for its TypeScript/JavaScript variants (typescript/javascript vs. the camelCase forms typeScript/javaScript that would result if the rule were camelCase instead) -- unlike DiagnosticKind (SPEC-006 AC-013), where the same rule distinction was observationally identical for all current variants, this cluster's Language enum makes the distinction concretely verifiable.
scope: SearchOptions (7 fields, hand-written Default, serde-inertness of that Default), SearchLimits (4 fields, hand-written Default, the same inertness plus its interaction with two Option<usize> fields' own independent leniency), Language (4-variant enum with dual independent naming systems -- serde's rename_all="lowercase" for the JSON wire format and clap's per-variant value(name=...) for the CLI, gated independently by #[cfg_attr(feature = "cli", ...)]), SearchResponse (7 fields, Serialize-only), SymbolsResult (4 fields, Serialize-only, including a BTreeMap-keyed result field and its deterministic key-ordering property), and DependentsResult (7 fields, Serialize-only) -- all verbatim per 01-core-architecture.md's Section 4 declarations for these six types. It locks: each type's exact field/variant order, derive list, and serde attributes; the precise scope of SearchOptions/SearchLimits' Default-impl inertness for deserialize purposes; SearchLimits' max_results/max_tokens divergence between JSON-omission (None) and Default-construction (Some(50)/Some(20_000)); Language's dual naming systems and the real camelCase/lowercase divergence for its TypeScript/JavaScript variants; the uniform absence of skip_serializing_if on every Vec field across the three Serialize-only result types (results, diagnostics, dependents, imports never omit their key even when empty); SymbolsResult.files' BTreeMap-produced deterministic (sorted-by-key) JSON object shape; and the connection between SymbolsResult.total_symbol_count / DependentsResult.diagnostics and two already-documented corpus findings (07's finding #13 and finding #1 respectively), scoped precisely to what those findings actually establish.
non_goals: All other Section 4 types not in this cluster -- SymbolKind/Visibility/SymbolEntry (SPEC-003), the dependency/export/JSX/LangData cluster (SPEC-005), the result/diagnostic primitives CodeBlock/RankedBlock/ParentContext/Diagnostic/DiagnosticKind/LineHit (SPEC-006), and TsconfigMode/WorkspaceOptions/ExtractRequest (a separate, later track).

SymbolEntry's own shape, referenced by SymbolsResult.files' value type -- already locked by SPEC-003; this track locks only that SymbolsResult.files' value type is Vec<SymbolEntry>, not SymbolEntry's own fields.

RankedBlock's and Diagnostic's own shapes, referenced by SearchResponse.results and every Serialize-only type's diagnostics field -- already locked by SPEC-006; this track locks only that these fields have those types.

The input query-parameter type (referenced only indirectly, by name, in docs/spec/07-edge-cases-and-failure-modes.md Part 1 finding #13's description of a files: Vec<Utf8PathBuf> parameter that isn't deduplicated) that supplies the file list a symbols query runs against -- that type is not among the verbatim declarations this track locks, and finding #13's root cause (missing dedup on that input) is out of scope here; this track states only the observable, in-scope consequence on SymbolsResult.files and total_symbol_count (AC-014).

Whether monokl's search/symbols/dependents command implementations actually construct SearchOptions/SearchLimits via their Default impl plus explicit CLI-argument overrides, via JSON deserialize of an agent-supplied options object, or both -- this spec locks each construction path's observable consequence (AC-002, AC-005) without asserting which path any specific caller uses.

Whether the divergence this spec documents between SearchLimits' JSON-omission defaults and its Default-impl defaults (AC-005) should be resolved (e.g. by adding #[serde(default)]) -- this spec states the current, verbatim behavior; deciding whether to change it is a behavioral decision for whichever track owns SearchLimits' construction paths.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: SearchOptions compiles with #[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)] and #[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")], with exactly 7 fields in this order: query: String, path: Utf8PathBuf, allow_tests: bool, no_gitignore: bool, limits: SearchLimits, exact: bool, language: Option<Language>. No field carries any field-level serde attribute. SearchOptions additionally carries a hand-written impl Default (not #[derive(Default)]) supplying query: String::new(), path: Utf8PathBuf::new(), allow_tests: false, no_gitignore: false, limits: SearchLimits::default(), exact: false, language: None.

SearchOptions' hand-written impl Default is completely inert for JSON deserialize: SearchOptions carries no container-level #[serde(default)] and no field-level #[serde(default)] on any of its 7 fields, and neither serde attribute appears anywhere in its declaration. Deriving Deserialize without either attribute means a missing JSON key is never filled in from the type's own Default impl -- that substitution only happens when #[serde(default)] (container-level, using the type's Default::default()) or a field-level #[serde(default)] explicitly requests it, and this struct requests neither. Structural consequence: because neither attribute is present, serde's derive-generated Deserialize impl treats query, path, allow_tests, no_gitignore, limits, and exact as required fields with no fallback source of any kind -- their Default-impl values are simply never consulted during deserialize. The specific, observable failure this produces for a JSON object omitting one of these keys is stated as its own dedicated error-case criterion in AC-003, not repeated here. language: Option<Language> is the sole exception, and only because Option<T>'s own Deserialize impl independently tolerates a missing or explicitly-null key (the pattern established in SPEC-003 AC-005) -- not because of anything SearchOptions' impl Default provides. For this one field, JSON-omission and Default-construction happen to produce the same value (None) purely because Option::default() is itself None -- a coincidence of this specific field's type, not evidence the struct's Default impl participates in deserialize at all. SearchOptions carries no #[serde(deny_unknown_fields)] attribute anywhere in its declaration (01-core-architecture.md:506-516): deserializing a JSON object that includes an extra key not among the 7 named in AC-001 succeeds, silently discarding the unrecognized key, the same unknown-key-tolerant behavior SPEC-003 AC-006 establishes for SymbolEntry and SPEC-006 AC-003/AC-010 establish for CodeBlock and Diagnostic.
acceptance_criteria.rationale: This is the same class of finding as SPEC-003's established #[non_exhaustive]-has-no-serde-effect result: a Rust-level construct (here, a hand-written impl Default) that a reader might assume interacts with serde's deserialize leniency, stated precisely as not doing so absent the specific attribute that would connect them. Marked judgment_call because the significance of stating this precisely (rather than assuming impl Default matters) is itself the finding, not a fact requiring interpretation.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: A JSON object being deserialized into SearchOptions that omits "query", "path", "allowTests", "noGitignore", "limits", or "exact" fails with a missing-field error naming that field, per AC-002. A "limits" value is handled by one of two independent contracts depending on its outer JSON type: a JSON object follows the object-form contract below; a JSON array follows the array-form contract below as an ORDERED two-step procedure, not a classification by array length alone -- element-type checking always runs first and can fail regardless of the array's length, and only once every checked element passes does length determine the outcome. Any other JSON type (string, integer, a number written with a fractional or exponent part, boolean, or null) fails immediately as a whole-value type mismatch. OBJECT-FORM CONTRACT: a "limits" object that is itself present but missing one of SearchLimits' own required keys ("maxBytes" or "maxCandidates") fails per AC-006's SearchLimits-specific missing-field error, not SearchOptions' own. WHOLE-VALUE TYPE-MISMATCH CONTRACT (applies to "limits": "default", "limits": 50, "limits": 1.5, "limits": true, "limits": null, and every JSON number literal): fails with "invalid type: <found>, expected struct SearchLimits" for every case except the number-out-of-range case noted below, where <found> is "string \"default\"" for a string, "boolean `true`" for a boolean, "null" for null, and for a JSON number, one of two forms depending on a three-way rule (serde_json never emits the token "number" for any of them): a number literal renders as "integer `N`" if and only if it has no fractional or exponent part AND its value fits within i64 or u64 range (0 to 18446744073709551615 unsigned, or down to -9223372036854775808 signed) -- "limits": 50 and "limits": 18446744073709551615 both render as "integer `50`"/"integer `18446744073709551615`". Otherwise, if the literal is finite when parsed as f64, it renders as "floating point `X`" regardless of whether its value happens to be a whole number: "limits": 1.5 renders as "floating point `1.5`", 5e2 as "floating point `500.0`", 50.0 as "floating point `50.0`", and -- the case that distinguishes this from a pure lexical-form rule -- an integer-lexical-form literal one past either integer boundary is ALSO reinterpreted as floating point: "limits": 18446744073709551616 (one past the u64 maximum) renders as "floating point `1.8446744073709552e+19`", and "limits": -9223372036854775809 (one past the i64 minimum) likewise renders as floating point, not integer. Otherwise, if the literal's magnitude exceeds finite f64 range entirely (e.g. "limits": 1e309), deserialization fails at parse time with "number out of range" before any type dispatch against struct SearchLimits occurs -- no "expected struct SearchLimits" text appears in this one case, unlike every other whole-value type mismatch in this contract. limits is SearchLimits, not Option<SearchLimits>, so null is treated the same as any other type-mismatched scalar rather than deserializing to any default-equivalent value, unlike language: Option<Language>, where null is valid. ARRAY-FORM CONTRACT, applied in this order for any JSON array value: STEP 1 (element-type check, always runs first) -- elements at positions 0 through min(array length, 4) - 1 are deserialized in order against their positional field's own type (position 0: max_results: Option<usize>; position 1: max_bytes: usize; position 2: max_tokens: Option<usize>; position 3: max_candidates: usize). The first element that fails its positional type produces an element-level error naming that field's own type -- usize, never struct SearchLimits or Option<usize> -- and this happens regardless of the array's total length, including arrays both shorter and longer than 4: "limits": ["a", 1, 2] fails with "invalid type: string \"a\", expected usize" (3 elements, but position 0 fails before length is ever considered); "limits": [1, -2, 3] fails with "invalid value: integer `-2`, expected usize"; "limits": [true] fails with "invalid type: boolean `true`, expected usize"; "limits": ["a", 1, 2, 3, 4] fails with "invalid type: string \"a\", expected usize" (5 elements, but position 0 still fails first -- the 5th element is never reached); "limits": [1, -2, 3, 4, 5] fails with "invalid value: integer `-2`, expected usize" for the same reason. The array is consumed strictly left to right, and the first failure encountered at the lowest element position wins, whether that failure is an ordinary positional type failure or a parse-level failure on the literal itself -- an out-of-range numeric literal is not an exception to first-failure-wins, it IS first-failure-wins, differing only in that its error text names no field type instead of naming usize. An element literal whose magnitude exceeds finite f64 range (e.g. position 1 of "limits": [1, 1e309, 3, 4]) fails with "number out of range" ONLY when no earlier position (here, position 0) already failed its own positional type check first: "limits": ["a", 1e309, 3, 4] fails with "invalid type: string \"a\", expected usize" at position 0, not "number out of range" at position 1, because position 0 is checked first and its failure wins regardless of what position 1 contains. An out-of-range literal at position 4 or beyond is never parsed at all, since STEP 1 only checks positions 0 through min(length, 4) - 1: "limits": [1, 2, 3, 4, 1e309] fails with "trailing characters", identically to "limits": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] (STEP 2's surplus-element rule below), not "number out of range" -- the out-of-range literal at position 4 is surplus input, never reached by STEP 1's per-element check at all. This is distinct from an integer-lexical-form element merely beyond u64 range within the checked positions, which does reach dispatch and produces the ordinary element-level error: "limits": [1, 18446744073709551616, 3, 4] yields "invalid type: floating point `1.8446744073709552e+19`, expected usize" at position 1, exactly as any other floating-point-rendered element would, since position 0 already passed its own check first. STEP 2 (length check, runs only if every checked element passed step 1) -- once positions 0 through min(length, 4) - 1 all type-check successfully, the array's length alone determines the outcome: fewer than 4 elements fails with "invalid length N, expected struct SearchLimits with 4 elements" ("limits": [] produces "invalid length 0"; "limits": [1, 2, 3] -- all 3 elements type-check -- produces "invalid length 3"); more than 4 elements does NOT fail with a length error, because serde's derived visit_seq for this 4-field struct consumes exactly 4 elements and returns without draining the remaining SeqAccess, so the surplus element(s) are never type-checked and surface to serde_json as unconsumed input, producing a trailing-characters syntax error instead ("limits": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] and "limits": [1, 2, 3, 4, "x"] both fail with "trailing characters", identically, since the 5th element's own type is never inspected); exactly 4 elements succeeds, deserializing positionally -- "limits": [50, 100, null, 5] deserializes to SearchLimits { max_results: Some(50), max_bytes: 100, max_tokens: None, max_candidates: 5 }, and "limits": [null, 2, null, 4] also succeeds (max_results: None, max_tokens: None) since positions 0 and 2 target Option<usize>, which accepts null positionally the same as it does by key in the object-form contract's AC-006 error surface.

SearchLimits compiles with #[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)] and #[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")], with exactly 4 fields in this order: max_results: Option<usize>, max_bytes: usize, max_tokens: Option<usize>, max_candidates: usize. No field carries any field-level serde attribute. SearchLimits additionally carries a hand-written impl Default (not #[derive(Default)]) supplying max_results: Some(50), max_bytes: 2_097_152, max_tokens: Some(20_000), max_candidates: 1_000.

SearchLimits' hand-written impl Default is, by the same mechanism as AC-002, completely inert for JSON deserialize: no container-level or field-level #[serde(default)] appears anywhere in its declaration. max_bytes and max_candidates (both usize, not Option) are strictly required on deserialize with no fallback source of any kind despite the Default impl supplying 2_097_152 and 1_000 respectively -- the specific, observable failure this produces is stated as its own dedicated error-case criterion in AC-006, not repeated here. max_results and max_tokens (both Option<usize>) tolerate a missing or explicitly-null key via Option<T>'s own independent Deserialize leniency (SPEC-003 AC-005) and default to None on omission -- not to Some(50) or Some(20_000), the values SearchLimits::default() would supply if constructed via Rust code instead of JSON deserialize. This is a genuine divergence, not a coincidence: for max_results and max_tokens specifically, an agent-supplied JSON object that omits both fields to signal "use the defaults" instead silently receives None (unbounded, per docs/spec/07-edge-cases-and-failure-modes.md Part 1 finding #11's observation that these two knobs have no ceiling) rather than the bounded Some(50)/Some(20_000) a Rust caller invoking SearchLimits::default() directly would receive for the identical intent -- the same nominal 'caller didn't specify a value' case resolves to two different outcomes depending on which construction path is used. This is additive to, not a restatement of, finding #11: finding #11 documents that max_results/max_tokens have no enforced ceiling once a value is present; this criterion documents that omitting them entirely does not even reach the Default impl's own bounded fallback value. SearchLimits carries no #[serde(deny_unknown_fields)] attribute anywhere in its declaration (01-core-architecture.md:532-539): deserializing a JSON object that includes an extra key not among the 4 named in AC-004 succeeds, silently discarding the unrecognized key, the same unknown-key-tolerant behavior established for SearchOptions above and for SPEC-003/SPEC-006's prior tracks.
acceptance_criteria.rationale: The distinction between 'no ceiling on a supplied value' (finding #11's claim) and 'omission doesn't reach the Default impl's fallback value at all' (this criterion's claim) is precise and non-overlapping, but both concern the same two fields and the same general theme of unbounded-by-construction resource limits -- flagged as a judgment call to make clear this is presented as a complementary, narrower observation rather than a re-discovery of finding #11 or a claim that finding #11 is incomplete.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: A JSON object being deserialized into SearchLimits that omits "maxBytes" or "maxCandidates" fails with a missing-field error naming that field, per AC-005. A JSON object where "maxBytes", "maxCandidates", "maxResults", or "maxTokens" holds a negative integer (e.g. -1) fails to deserialize with an invalid-value error, since serde_json's integer deserialization for unsigned target types (usize) rejects negative source values outright -- the same out-of-range behavior SPEC-003 AC-012 establishes for SymbolEntry.line and SPEC-006 AC-003 establishes for CodeBlock's usize fields, and the same for maxResults/maxTokens despite their Option<usize> wrapper: the Option only governs whether the key may be absent, not what happens when a present value is out of range for the wrapped usize. A JSON object where any of these same four fields holds a JSON number that is not a valid non-negative usize also fails to deserialize, via the same three-way rule AC-003's whole-value contract states for "limits" itself, applied here against usize rather than struct SearchLimits: a number literal with no fractional or exponent part that fits within u64 range (0 to 18446744073709551615) succeeds as the corresponding usize value; a number literal with no fractional or exponent part that is negative but fits within i64 range (down to -9223372036854775808) fails with an invalid-value error ("invalid value: integer `-1`, expected usize") -- the same class the negative-integer case above produces; any number literal written with a fractional or exponent part (e.g. 2097152.5, 2097152.0, 2e6 -- regardless of whether its value happens to be a whole number) fails with an invalid-type error ("invalid type: floating point `2097152.5`, expected usize"), a different error class than the invalid-value case, not "the same reason"; an integer-lexical-form literal one past either the u64 maximum or the i64 minimum (18446744073709551616 or -9223372036854775809) is reinterpreted as floating point and fails the same invalid-type way; and a literal whose magnitude exceeds finite f64 range entirely (e.g. 1e309) fails at parse time with "number out of range" before any type dispatch, naming neither usize nor any other type -- three rejection classes in total (invalid-value, invalid-type, and number-out-of-range), not two. A JSON object with "maxResults": null or "maxTokens": null deserializes both to None, identically to omitting the key entirely -- distinct from a present out-of-range value for either field, which fails per the three error classes stated above rather than falling back to None.

Language compiles with #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)], #[serde(rename_all = "lowercase")], and #[cfg_attr(feature = "cli", derive(clap::ValueEnum))], with exactly 4 variants in this order: TypeScript (carrying #[cfg_attr(feature = "cli", value(name = "typescript"))]), JavaScript (carrying #[cfg_attr(feature = "cli", value(name = "javascript"))]), Rust (carrying #[cfg_attr(feature = "cli", value(name = "rust"))]), Python (carrying #[cfg_attr(feature = "cli", value(name = "python"))]). No #[non_exhaustive]. The clap::ValueEnum derive and every per-variant value(name = ...) attribute are conditional on the "cli" feature via #[cfg_attr]: with that feature disabled, Language does not implement clap::ValueEnum at all, and the value(name = ...) attributes are stripped entirely at compile time -- attempting to use Language as a clap value type in a build without the "cli" feature is a compile-time error, not a runtime one. The #[derive(..., Serialize, Deserialize)] and #[serde(rename_all = "lowercase")] attributes are unconditional and apply regardless of the "cli" feature's state.

Language's #[serde(rename_all = "lowercase")] lowercases each variant name's every character uniformly with no word-boundary handling (the same rule DiagnosticKind uses, SPEC-006 AC-013), producing exactly "typescript", "javascript", "rust", "python" for the 4 variants on serialize. Unlike DiagnosticKind, where "lowercase" and "camelCase" happen to produce identical output for all current variants, Language's TypeScript and JavaScript variants make the distinction concretely observable, not merely hypothetical: had Language instead carried #[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")] (it does not), TypeScript would produce "typeScript" (only the leading character lowercased, the internal capital S preserved) and JavaScript would produce "javaScript" (identically), both different from the "lowercase" rule's actual "typescript"/"javascript" output -- Rust and Python, being single words, would produce identical output under either rule regardless. This is a real, verifiable divergence between the two rules for this specific enum, not an illustrative aside about a variant the spec doesn't add.

Language's JSON wire-format naming (governed by #[serde(rename_all = "lowercase")], unconditional) and its CLI value naming (governed by clap's per-variant #[cfg_attr(feature = "cli", value(name = ...))], conditional) are two independently configured, independently maintained attribute mechanisms with no shared source of truth enforcing consistency between them -- serde's macro does not read clap's value(name = ...) attributes and clap's macro does not read serde's rename_all attribute. For Language's current 4 variants, both mechanisms happen to produce identical strings ("typescript"/"javascript"/"rust"/"python" from both the JSON wire format and the CLI value name), but this is a property of the two attributes having been set to matching literal strings, not a guarantee either macro enforces -- changing one attribute's string (e.g. a future CLI value(name = "ts")) would not propagate to or be validated against the other.
acceptance_criteria.rationale: Stating that two independent mechanisms currently agree, without either enforcing agreement with the other, is a precise structural observation about the type as declared -- not a prediction that they will diverge, and not a recommendation to unify them, which would be a design decision out of this track's scope.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: Language carries no #[serde(other)] fallback and no #[non_exhaustive]. Deserializing a JSON string value that does not exactly match "typescript", "javascript", "rust", or "python" -- including any camelCase-style value that would diverge under the two naming rules per AC-008, such as "typeScript" -- fails with a serde unknown-variant error.

SearchResponse compiles with #[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize)] -- Serialize only, no Deserialize -- and #[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")], with exactly 7 fields in this order: results: Vec<RankedBlock>, total_blocks_before_truncation: usize, truncated: bool, truncation_marker: Option<String>, total_bytes: usize, total_tokens: usize, diagnostics: Vec<Diagnostic>. No field carries any field-level serde attribute. Because SearchResponse has no Deserialize impl, it can never be parsed from JSON, and because its results field's element type RankedBlock also has no Deserialize impl (SPEC-006 AC-005), there is no inconsistency between SearchResponse's own lack of Deserialize and its contained element type's lack of Deserialize -- had RankedBlock derived Deserialize while SearchResponse attempted to as well, that would still compile independently of this fact, since Vec<T>'s Deserialize only requires T: Deserialize, not the reverse. truncation_marker: Option<String>, like every other bare Option<T> field established in this project's prior tracks, always emits its key with a JSON null value when None rather than omitting it.

None of SearchResponse.results, SearchResponse.diagnostics, SymbolsResult.diagnostics, DependentsResult.dependents, DependentsResult.imports, or DependentsResult.diagnostics carries #[serde(skip_serializing_if = "Vec::is_empty")] or any other field-level serde attribute -- every one of these six Vec fields across this cluster's three Serialize-only result types always emits its key in serialize output, as an explicit empty JSON array, even when the Vec is empty. This is a direct, verifiable contrast to CodeBlock.matched_lines and CodeBlock.matched_keywords (SPEC-006 AC-002), which do carry skip_serializing_if and omit their key entirely when empty. #[serde(default)] would have no effect on any of these six fields even if present, since none of these three types derive Deserialize -- default is a deserialize-only attribute with nothing to act on here.

SymbolsResult compiles with #[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize)] -- Serialize only, no Deserialize -- and #[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")], with exactly 4 fields in this order: files: BTreeMap<Utf8PathBuf, Vec<SymbolEntry>>, total_symbol_count: usize, truncation_marker: Option<String>, diagnostics: Vec<Diagnostic>. No field carries any field-level serde attribute. files' Serialize output is a JSON object (not an array) whose keys are each Utf8PathBuf's string form and whose values are JSON arrays of SymbolEntry objects (SPEC-003's shape, not re-locked here); because files is a BTreeMap rather than a HashMap, its keys serialize in the order induced by Utf8PathBuf's own Ord implementation (required for BTreeMap<Utf8PathBuf, _> to compile at all) -- for a given set of file paths, that key order is identical on every run and every machine, a positive contrast to docs/spec/07-edge-cases-and-failure-modes.md Part 1 finding #10's documented non-determinism in this project's candidate-selection walk order elsewhere in the corpus. This criterion does not itself define what that ordering rule is (e.g. whether it is raw string comparison or path-component-aware comparison, which can disagree for paths like "a/b" versus "ab") -- the rule is intrinsic to Utf8PathBuf's own Ord implementation (the camino crate), not something SymbolsResult's declaration overrides or restates; only the determinism property (same input always produces the same order) is this criterion's claim.
acceptance_criteria.rationale: Stating determinism (falsifiable by re-running the same input and comparing output) without also asserting the specific comparison rule (which would require independently confirming camino's Ord implementation, out of scope for a type-shape lock) keeps the criterion testable without overclaiming knowledge of a mechanism this spec doesn't own.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: docs/spec/01-core-architecture.md:2546, in this track's own primary source document, prescribes a named integration test -- symbols_total_count_is_accurate -- asserting total_symbol_count == sum(file.values().map(Vec::len)): the invariant that SymbolsResult.total_symbol_count equals the sum of each Vec<SymbolEntry>'s length across every entry in files IS mandated as a required test, not left unstated. SymbolsResult itself provides no type-level mechanism enforcing this invariant -- files and total_symbol_count are two independently-populated fields with nothing in their declaration (AC-013) connecting one to the other, so a SymbolsResult value violating the invariant is not rejected by deserialize or by any constructor this spec locks (SymbolsResult has no Deserialize impl at all, per AC-013, so this can only happen via direct construction, not JSON input). docs/spec/07-edge-cases-and-failure-modes.md Part 1 finding #13 documents a concrete construction path that violates the mandated invariant despite the prescribed test: a duplicate path in the (out-of-scope, not locked by this track) input file-list parameter causes the later occurrence to overwrite the earlier one when inserted into the files BTreeMap -- collapsing what were two separate per-file symbol counts into one map entry -- while total_symbol_count is computed independently and does not correct for the collapse, "breaking the spec's own asserted invariant." This track does not resolve the root cause (deduplicating the input parameter, out of scope per non_goals) but states precisely that the invariant is mandated by test, not enforced by the type, and that finding #13 documents a concrete input under which the mandated invariant is actually violated.
acceptance_criteria.rationale: The invariant's status flipped from an assumed absence to a confirmed, source-mandated test requirement once docs/spec/01-core-architecture.md:2546 was checked directly rather than only checking docs/spec/07-edge-cases-and-failure-modes.md for prior documentation -- the same class of error as SPEC-006 AC-004's original overreach (checking one document for novelty while missing that the primary source itself already covers the ground), corrected here by canon-exit-gate rather than canon-verifier. Marked judgment_call because scoping the claim to 'mandated by test, not enforced by type, violated by a concrete out-of-scope input' required care not to overstate what this track can resolve.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: DependentsResult compiles with #[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize)] -- Serialize only, no Deserialize -- and #[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")], with exactly 7 fields in this order: file: Utf8PathBuf, dependents: Vec<Utf8PathBuf>, imports: Vec<Utf8PathBuf>, total_dependent_count: usize, total_import_count: usize, truncation_marker: Option<String>, diagnostics: Vec<Diagnostic>. No field carries any field-level serde attribute.

DependentsResult.diagnostics is the same Diagnostic-typed field (SPEC-006 AC-010) that docs/spec/07-edge-cases-and-failure-modes.md Part 1 finding #1 discusses directly by name: per finding #1's verified correction (already established in SPEC-006 AC-011), WorkspaceIndex -- the structure dependents' implementation is described as routing through -- has no diagnostics field of its own at all, and finding #1 states explicitly that dependents "has nothing comparable to route a dropped-file signal into DependentsResult.diagnostics." revision_note: First draft, produced under the same corner-case-first methodology established for SPEC-006: enumerated per-type corner cases (missing/null/wrong-type/extra-field, boundary values, cross-field invariants, sibling-type interactions, and -- new for this cluster -- the interaction between a type's own hand-written impl Default and its serde deserialize contract) before writing any criterion. The central finding this methodology surfaced before drafting began: SearchOptions and SearchLimits both have a hand-written impl Default with specific documented values, and neither carries #[serde(default)] anywhere, so those defaults never reach a JSON deserialize call -- a distinction a bare transcription of the struct fields would very plausibly have missed, since a reader who sees 'this type has sensible defaults' would reasonably but wrongly assume a missing JSON key falls back to them.
reasoning: This track's central technical risk, identified before drafting: a hand-written impl Default is a Rust-level construct entirely independent of serde's deserialize machinery unless a specific #[serde(default)] attribute (container- or field-level) explicitly wires them together -- and this project has already gotten burned once by assuming a Rust-level attribute participates in serde's behavior when it does not (SPEC-003's #[non_exhaustive]-has-no-serde-effect finding). Rather than assume analogously that impl Default's presence implies deserialize leniency, I checked the verbatim declaration for #[serde(default)] specifically and confirmed its total absence on both SearchOptions and SearchLimits before asserting AC-002/AC-005's inertness claims. The max_results/max_tokens divergence (AC-005) is the most load-bearing finding in this track: JSON-omission and Default-construction give genuinely different fallback values (None vs. Some(50)/Some(20_000)) for the identical 'caller didn't specify' intent -- worth stating with precision since getting the direction of this claim wrong (e.g. claiming JSON-omission also reaches Some(50)) would be exactly the kind of confident-but-wrong serde claim this project's history warns against; the empirical toolchain verification stage should confirm this precisely before the spec gates. AC-008's Language lowercase-vs-camelCase divergence deliberately extends SPEC-006 AC-013's necessarily-hypothetical illustration (DiagnosticKind's 3 variants never actually diverge under the two rules) into a concretely verifiable case using this cluster's own TypeScript/JavaScript variants -- worth cross-referencing explicitly since it turns what was previously stated as a plausible-but-untested claim into a directly checkable one. AC-014 and AC-016 both cite findings whose root cause lives partly or wholly outside this track's locked types (an unlocked input-parameter type for AC-014, an unlocked WorkspaceIndex structure for AC-016) -- both were scoped carefully to state only the observable, in-scope consequence on this track's own fields, explicitly not claiming to resolve or fully own the out-of-scope cause, learning directly from SPEC-006 AC-004 and AC-011's initial overreach (caught by canon-verifier) before either criterion was drafted rather than after.
